subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF COAL MINES AND WATER
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, measures should be taken to regain for the use of the people the coal mines and water-powers which are now being exploited in the interest of private corporations rather than for the needs of the people.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the suggestion was
made on Friday that some of the hon. members opposite would like to proceed with certain resolutions to-day, but we have no definite assurance that we will have another Monday, and I would not like to allow this opportunity to pass without presenting this important resolution to the House. I have every desire to meet the convenience of my hon. friends opposite, however, and while I cannot control the debate I shall be very well satisfied if it is adjourned before six o'clock, to give hon. gentlemen opposite an opportunity to proceed.
It is sometimes charged that resolutions of this character are academic. I might point out that they are academic simply because we have not as yet a sufficient number of people thinking along these lines to bring these policies into operation. I have not the slightest doubt that before very many years have passed these questions will come decidedly within the realm of practical politics. In this particular case, however, my resolution has a very topical interest because of the developments which have taken place in recent weeks in the district immediately adjacent to the capital city.
For once I find myself in sympathy with the Toronto Telegram, and I hope the Toronto Telegram will note that fact. In the issue of April 15 the Telegram calls attention to the fact that since Sir Adam Beck's death private interests have been gradually resuming their encroachments, particularly in northern Ontario. By means of an agreement announced recently, for a supply of 260,000 horse power from Quebec, they have secured, according to the Telegram, a foothold in eastern Ontario, and have even reached as far as Toronto. Let me quote a paragraph:
A thirty year contract for a supply of power from private interests in Quebec means the end of Sir

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF COAL MINES AND WATER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much impressed by the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (M'r. Woods-worth). I also regret the fact that the situation in Ontario is such that Ontario power interests have had to go outside of the province for a source of power for distribution within the province. I do not know where the blame ought to be laid, but I sympathize with the Toronto Telegram in its expression of dissent from what has taken place and that the province had been forced to go outside of the province for power when it might have been generated at home absolutely under the control and ownership of Ontario which has led the world in public-ownership development and distribution of power throughout the province. Still, there is some relief coming from a privately-owned company in Ottawa, and I cannot complain of that although there is a suspicion in Toronto and throughout the province that in some way privately-owned companies have been rather conspiring in that regard.
I want to say a word about the power situation in Great Britain. As a believer in public ownership I regret that Great Britain has not followed the example of Ontario and developed a great system of public ownership and distribution of power,

The former speaker also referred to pooling interests. I am not going into the matter in detail to-day, but I hope to do so later on in this House. If you deal with the transportation problem, you must deal with it as a whole. It will not do to deal with railways and to neglect transportation now performed by waterways, nor the future transportation of goods by airways. In other words, if you want to deal with the transportation problem to-day, the world has moved so fast that you cannot solve it properly unless you deal with it from every angle. To build up our ports and railways you have to go further, you have to find out not only how you can improve transportation by dealing with your railways, but you must also deal with the three or four or more manifestations of transportation and1 pool them. To-day you must pool things if you want to succeed. It is only by employing them all that you can make any headway.
I had something to do with the dream of the Niagara power development. It was made fun of at the time and Adam Beck was almost called a lunatic and discouraged in every way; but our dream came true. Now, I have a dream similar to that described by the preceding speaker (Mr. Woodsworth). I agree with him that on the Hudson slope we have the greatest potential water powers in

the world. The people of Canada own them, but there are men in the United States and elsewhere, men with vast financial resources at their back, ready to grab these great national assets. Long distance high tension transmission is coming very rapidly. We have these and other great potential resources of electric energy, some owned by the provinces and some by the Dominion, but as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, we must get the necessary legislation to enable us to handle them. Our constitution, drafted sixty years ago, is rather an old-fashioned instrument, and we have not the means in our own hands of amending it. It will be said by some hon. members: You are suggesting separation from England. I am suggesting nothing of the kind. But I want to see the parliament of Canada made so efficient that it can deal with this and other problems as they arise. These great national problems we are not able to deal with under our present constitution. Last week, for instance, we found we were hampered in dealing with old age pensions. The same incapacity handicaps us in dealing with our power problem. All these questions broaden as the years pass, and this parliament should be in a position to deal adequately with our national problems, especially those which, solved in the proper way, will make life more livable for every Canadian citizen. Our opponents want to monopolize these vital public services for their own financial benefit rather than for the advantage of the people.
I agree largely with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said in connection with this question, and I have thrown out a suggestion to my friends from Nova Scotia. As one member of this House, I am ready to back up Nova Scotia in a publicly-owned development of her coal mines and the distribution of power generated by steam plants at their pit heads, the generation and distribution to be undertaken by the province as a public ownership enterprise. I wish to see Nova Scotia given a chance to work out this great problem right at home. Many of those who want the Dominion to aid such enterprises desire the aid to go to private individuals. I am not in favour of that, but I am ready to back up Nova Scotia to-morrow if she will go ahead and solve this problem on a public ownership basis. I would also like to see her go into the coking business so as to produce coke in sufficient quantities to ship to Quebec and to Ontario, for as I see it the fuel market of the central provinces belongs to Nova Scotia, I would not like

Socialization of Natural Resources
to see this developed as a means of private profit but rather in the direction of service to all the people, and for that reason I have trespassed on the time of the House for a few minutes in making these suggestions.
Capital is becoming so strongly entrenched that the legislatures of the country, whether provincial or Dominion, must take great care to protect the public domain. Fortunately no monopoly, however securely it may seem to be founded, is impregnable, for undoubtedly scientific development will eventually render many present types of machinery obsolete. The surprise of the world to-day is not what science is doing now but what it will be doing to-morrow, and what it will be doing tomorrow may be in the direction of scrapping the very things behind which capital has entrenched itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution proposes :
'That, in the opinion of this House, measures should be taken to regain for the use of the people the coal mines and water-powers which are now being exploited in the interest of private corporations rather than for the needs of the people.
I submit, Sir, that in so far as Canada is concerned the coal mines and water powers which are now being "exploited"-I prefer "operated"-are being operated for the use of the people. There is a clear distinction between the views of the people in the province of which I represent a constituency and those of the people of Ontario. In our province we believe in developing industry by individual initiative, individual enterprise, individual management, under public supervision and control. I do not wish to precipitate a contest of opinion as to the merits of the hydro-electric services of Ontario and the hydro-electric services of Quebec, but if there were time and opportunity I think I could vindicate before any independent tribunal the opinion which we in that province entertain, that our services are cheap, stable and well managed and serve the public interest to an extent that has not yet been achieved in the province of Ontario. So long as the people of the province of Quebec entertain that opinion, I think it is expedient that they should be allowed to proceed along their own lines, pursuing their own ideals and accomplishing the results which they have in view, and which are very necessary for the prosperity of the industries of that great province. Therefore perhaps it is that the Fathers of Confederation in framing the British North America Act left property and civil rights within the control of provincial
legislatures, so that the legislature immediately responsible to the people of each province could be guided by the opinion of that province both with respect to industrial development and to such developments as coal mines and water powers.
The situation of Canada at the present time is that the development of hydro-electric power and energy for lighting and power purposes in each of the provinces is controlled and directed and supervised by commissions appointed by the governments of those several provinces. There you have a very effective control. It is true that we have vested in the crown, as represented by the Dominion government, large water powers in the territories which undoubtedly are soon to be vested in the several provincial legislatures, but I will say that I do not believe any department of the Dominion government is more honestly and more efficiently managed, supervised and controlled than is the Water Powers branch.

At that time one might well have advocated government monopoly in the production and use of sperm oil. In 1900 electric lighting was introduced, and since that time there has been in many districts municipal ownership of electric lighting plants. In other districts such plants are operated by private companies, but I venture to say that in the United States to-day, where private companies are operating under reasonably sound municipal or state supervision, you would not find the people adopting public ownership of lighting plants. speechtext: May I ask if the coal mining industry has been efficient in either the eastern or the western part of this country?

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF COAL MINES AND WATER
speechtext:
I think that coal mining in Nova Scotia and in Alberta, about which I know something, is being done fairly efficiently. The great difficulty with coal mining in Canada to-day is that it is a seasonal occupation. I went through the strike in 1909
in Cape Breton; I was through it from beginning to end, and I came in contact with all the various opinions prevalent there. Last summer I had the opportunity of discussing that same problem with a number of very intelligent men from that province, and I believe-it is my individual opinion-that the difficulty in Cape Breton arises from the fact that the employment in the mines is not continuous and stable. I do not believe there is a miner in Cape Breton to-day but would accept a lower wage, and give a greater output per man, if he could be assured that, instead of being employed for only five or six months of the year in mining, he could be employed during the whole twelve months, save for an occasional holiday that might be necessary. That is the difficulty in Cape Breton, so far as coal mining is concerned. Change that from a seasonal occupation to a continuous occupation throughout the year, for which and during which the miners would be paid, a reasonable wage, and lower than they are being paid to-day, would be acceptable if the employment were continuous, and the difficulty would be largely solved.
But further-I am talking as an amateur who is interested in this subject, having jotted down some notes while my hon. friend was speaking-the chief difficulty does not arise out of the mining of coal; the difficulty arises out of the utilization of the coal after it is mined. What I mean in this: There is no more wasteful habit that could be possibly cultivated by the people of Canada than the burning of raw coals in their hearths, in their stoves, or for the production of steam power. If my memory is right, every ton of good bituminous coal sacrifices, when burnt in the oven, at the hearth or in the furnace, 11,000 cubic feet of gas, 9 gallons of tar, 25 pounds of ammonium sulphate, 2.08 gallons of pure benzol and .56 gallons of pure toluol, and if we could establish plants in this country for the production of coke, and use that coke for the production of heat and of steam, and utilize these by-products which are now wasted and sacrificed, the value of these by-products would cut down the price of coal for industrial purposes in this country to a point lower than it has been during the past twenty years.
There is the difficulty. It may be that, in order to utilize the coal, government assistance may be helpful along certain lines, but government acquisition and government management of the coal mines in the present political conditions of this country-I hardly

know what word to use, but it is practically impossible to do it honestly and efficiently under governments and under political parties as they are now constituted in this country.

I
quite agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken that we are on the eve of very great and important changes in hydro-electric development. I quite expect to see, even within my own lifetime, some tremendous changes in that regard. I hope to see within the very near future-I fully expect to see it-the transmission of hydro-electric energy without the use of transmission wires. Experts are now getting very close to the point in their experiments where it will 'be possible to transmit electric energy for very long distances without the use of wires. When that comes about it will mean a tremendous revolution in hydro-electric development in all parts of the continent.
The previous speaker made one or two references which I cannot allow to pass unchallenged. He stated that under private ownership there is a certain amount of initiative which you are hardly likely to have under public ownership. I think I am quoting the hon. gentleman correctly. With that particular statement of his I am bound to take issue. I come from a city where we have quite a large hydro-electric undertaking which is entirely publicly owned and publicly controlled. There is no commission in charge

Socialization of Natural Resources
of it, it is controlled by the city council of Winnipeg. Before Winnipeg went into its own hydro-electric development the people of that city were paying 20 cents per kilowatt hour. The moment it became mooted that the city was about to develop its own electric energy and supply it to the people the price came down to 10 cents per kilowatt hour. When the civic hydro-electric development became an actual fact the city council supplied the people with electricity at 3J cents per kilowatt hour. In addition to that there was a 10 per cent discount. Now the average rate of hydro-electric energy to the domestic consumer in that city is just slightly over two *cents per kilowatt hour. There is no privately-owned concern on the continent which can -compare in the matter of initiative with the publicly-owned utility of the city of Winnipeg. I say that because for a number of years I had some connection with it, being a member of the Winnipeg city council. In fact so enterprising is the management of -this utility that the opponents of public ownership are always on the alert and always on- the move to try and check the initiative which it displays at varioiis times.
Now what have we done with this publicly-owned utility?	I wish	to	say that we areeven ahead of	the city	of	Toronto in	thatregard. What is the use of a publicly-owned utility unless it can give better service than one which is privately-owned? I say that these publicly-owned utilities can and do give better service than privately-owned concerns no matter in what part	of	the country	theyhappen to be.	If they	were not doing	that
there would be no publicly-owned utilities. Now, our own public utility in Winnipeg, in addition to giving one of the lowest rates of any prevailing on the American- continent, has introduced the very latest developments in hydro-electric enterprise into the homes of the people. Housewives, who at one time found their work a drudgery, have experienced great vel-ief as a result of the enterprise which has been shown by our hydro-electric system. I think I am correct in stating that there are more electric appliances used in Winnipeg than are to be found in any other city of the same size in any part of the world. In the city of Winnipeg there are several places where these electric appliances may be bought on easy terms by the people. Each year private corporations in that city have complained because the civic hydro-electric management can sell at a lower rate and give better service than private corporations.
What else have we done in Winnipeg? In addition to bringing about a most important *electrical development there we have done
something which no other city in Canada has done as yet. As the result of our electrical development Winnipeg has the first publicly-owned central heating system in the Dominion. There are approximately one hundred of the large buildings in the centre of the city which are heated from the central heating system, and perhaps it would be of interest to hon. members to find out how that came about. A few years ago Winnipeg was troubled very much by the storms which blew down the transmission lines between Pointe du Bois, where we get our hydroelectric energy, and the city. Accordingly it was decided to establish a steam standby plant so that at any time when the wires were down the city should not be without a continuous hydro-electric service. Following the establishment of that standby plant we installed a central heating system so that the boilers necessary for the steam standby plant could also be used for the purposes of a central heating system. The consequence is, as I have already mentioned, that a very large portion of the centre of Winnipeg is now heated by the central heating plant. What is more important than that is the fact that as a result of our having that plant in Winnipeg there are certain times of the year when we do not use even one ounce of coal to heat a very large portion of the city. The heating of these buildings in the centre of Winnipeg is done by hydro-electric energy which comes a distance of 78 miles over transmission lines, and by the white fuel, as we term it. We heat a very large portion of the city at times by the utilization of off peak power, when it would otherwise be necessary to use coal. Now no private enterprise in this country has gone as far with this form of public utility as the city of Winnipeg. No other city in Canada has a central heating plant attached to its electrical development and can utilize the off peak power to heat buildings. Hon. members tell us that under public ownership there is less initiative than under private ownership. One fact mentioned by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) was that $650,000 was paid by the Montreal Light Heat and Power Company in income tax. I wonder where they got the $650,000? And when they paid that amount in income tax, I wonder how much their profits must have been for the year? If they had no profit, they would never have paid that money. But there is one thing, that where we have a publicly-owned utility, as we have in Winnipeg, or as they have in Ontario, if any profits are earned, those profits go to the consumer. In Montreal, if I remember my figures correctly-and I can be

Socialization oj Natural Resources
corrected if I am wrong-the cost to the consumer is about twice as much as it is in the city of Winnipeg. In Winnipeg, which is about one-fifth the size of Montreal, our total revenue from the sale of hydro-electric energy amounts to approximately $2,000,000 per annum, and, assuming that three times the quantity of electricity is sold in Montreal as in Winnipeg, it would amount to $6,000,000. Hon. members can easily figure out how much more the people of Montreal are paying for their light, heat and power, and can understand why the private corporation in Montreal is able to pay $660,000 income tax. I might give one other instance in regard to what we call initiative. I sometimes wonder what hon. members mean when they use that word. It is rather a difficult word to try to understand, and one would think from what we hear, that it was only in private ownership that there was an initiative. In other words, I would understand it to mean that a man shows initiative when he is working for a private corporation in order that he might make additional gain or profits. I think I am correct in /that assertion. But, Mr. Speaker, there are to-day professions where people study, give their energy, give the best that is in them and give their very life, where there is not one cent of profit to them. There are men practising in the medical profession who come under that category. It is one of the traditions of the men and women who work in that profession, who give of their talents, their skill and their lives, that they shall not receive one cent of reward for anything they may discover as the result of their own private initiative.

speechtext: The men of the medical profession have for years laboured hard, and when they discover something of benefit to humanity, they give it to the world without any reward, except perhaps the honour or glory that is bestowed on the man or woman who makes the particular discovery. But men of the medical profession have laboured because they thought they might render a service to mankind.

speechtext:
Yes, many men have worked for the benefit of humanity. It has been a time honoured custom with men of that class that when they have discovered something they have never attempted to commercialize it. We all know and recognize that fact. Then if it is possible in the medical profession it is possible in other lines of activity as well. When hon. members say that under public ownership there can be no initiative, I think they have not given sufficient study to the meaning of that word in relation to public and private enterprise.
No hon. member in this House who understands the development of public utilities in this country or any other country can rise in his place and defend private enterprise. Why it was private enterprise that gave us the Canadian National railway. It was the muddle and mess that private ownership made of that undertaking that compelled the government to take hold of it. If private enterprise is so beneficial to a country, why did they not make a success of it before it came into the hands of the government? The resolution placed before
the House by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, measures should be taken to regain for the use of the people the coal mines and water-powers which are now being exploited in the interest of private corporations rather than for the needs of the people.
I do not intend to detain the House more than a few moments, nor do I intend to espouse the cause of private or public ownership, but simply to point out some of the difficulties which we must meet in connection with a resolution of this kind. One of the first difficulties is that under the Act of Confederation those public utilities which are mentioned in the resolution remain under the control of the provincial government. But I agree with my hon. friends who have spoken that a great deal can be done to bring about uniformity in the mining of coal, for example, and uniformity in connection with the development of water-powers. The province of Ontario perhaps is the great, outstanding example of the utilization of electrical energy by public

Socialization oj Natural Resources
enterprise, and has given the lead in that direction. There are other provinces which have not followed in their footsteps up to the moment, but Ontario is the outstanding example of the development of this public utility under provincial government auspices. The federal government controls the natural resources of the three prairie provinces. In Alberta we have coal mines carried on to a very considerable extent and in the other provinces we have the development of water-powers. I intend to speak only of what the federal government has done in this connection. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out, the federal government no longer sells our natural resources; it issues leases which carry very strict provisions for a certain number of years for the development of (waten-powers and the same thing prevails in connection with coal mines. The privately-owned coal mines in Alberta were disposed of years ago; none has been disposed of in that manner since 1907. The stage is all set, if needs Ibe and if unanimity of opinion should prevail with the provinces for the development of coal mines, if you will, under public auspices. The same condition prevails in Nova Scotia where coal mines are owned by the provincial government and operated under private enterprise.
I want to speak for a moment of what we have been able to do in connection with the preservation of the forest wealth of the country. The same condition prevails. The provincial governments, with the exception of the three prairie provinces, own and control their forest wealth. In my attempt to get uniformity of action I found a great deal of suspicion abroad in the minds of the provincial authorities, and I admit that the feeling is sometimes too prevalent that there is a desire on the part of the federal authorities to interfere with provincial rights. The provincial authorities are always jealous and suspicious of their provincial rights and perhaps they have a right to be. But in the case of forestry we simply had to mention the fact that more forest wealth was being destroyed in Canada by fire and insect pests than we were manufacturing and selling in the finished state and we were bound to take some action hoping in some way to stem that devastation of our forest wealth. We began to approach the problem three or four years ago from the angle of inviting annually to conferences representatives of the provincial governments. We have accomplished a great deal in this way and we have 'learned a great deal from the provincial officials. But what we are aiming to do and will have done
within a very short period is to have a uniform system of cutting from one end of Canada to the other. We have not accomplished as much as we would like to do, but we have made splendid progress in that direction and I think we are at the stage now where we can change our own system of forestry. In other words, we can take the control of cutting which formerly was under the Timber branch of the Department of the Interior and put it under the control of the Forestry branch. Let me mention one recent lease issued in Manitoba for cutting pulp-wood. In that lease provision was made for reforestation of the area as it was cut. In other words, the cut will be over a period of twenty-five years under reforestation regulations which will renew the growth in twenty-five years so that you will have a perpetual forest for the maintenance of the mill. These are some of the things we have been able to accomplish by the simple expedient of getting representatives of the provinces to meet with the federal authorities and to agree on a uniform system of handling this great natural resource of Canada.
I believe a great deal could be accomplished in the same way for the coal mines. Very few of the provinces are selling their water-powers in toto to-day.; they are nearly all leasing them, and probably the day will come when the provinces themselves will think it is good business to operate their water-powers and electrical systems as Ontario is doing and as the federal government is doing in a much larger way in the operation of the Canadian National Railways. The primary object behind anything I have been advocating or been able to accomplish in this connection is to conserve to the people who come after us this great natural wealth which we own in such abundance in this country. We know beyond question of doubt that coal is being mined to-day in a most extravagant manner and we are making examination into a better method of coal mining in order that that natural resource may not be dissipated at such a rate as it is going to-day.
Something has been said-and I think a great deal more may be said-upon the subject of investigation and study of better methods for the conservation of our natural resources and the manufacture of them. We have in the departments of the federal government-and the same thing is true of the provincial governments-a body of men who are zealously carrying on this work. More and more our attention is being directed towards it; more and more research work is being carried on, and while we spend a great

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) has presented a question of very great importance with marked clearness from the standpoint of the western provinces. This question affects very materially the prosperity and wellbeing of the eastern provinces and of our Maritime ports. It vitally affects also the railways because it relates to their traffic, and the conditions under which that business
Transcontinental-Freight Rate

is carried on will determine whether a profit or a loss will be made. The grain-growing interest in the west-and it is a great satisfaction to us from the east to observe that this interest has expanded in recent years and assumed such great proportions,-is handicapped by reason of the tremendously long haul by railway necessary to get to tidewater, and then the long ocean carriage involved in reaching the markets of the world. Hence the question of transportation is one of very great importance to this country. In my judgment it is one of national importance, and one that should be carefully studied by parliament with a view of arriving at a sound, sane Canadian national policy. Having concluded what that policy should be, we should press forward earnestly and determinedly in carrying it out.
It may not be inopportune to consider, even at some little length, the efforts that have been made during the years that have passed -in connection with our transportation policy. We did not arrive at our transportation system as a result of one year or even ten years of effort. Fifty years ago and more we began the construction of a great transportation system in Canada when, by means of the Intercolonial railway the effort was made to bridge a gap of 500 miles of forest between the Maritime provinces and Quebec. That was the first step in the construction of a transportation system in Canada. We took a further Step when, ambitious and courageous, if you like, we undertook years ago to finance the construction of a railway across the continent, to span the prairies, to cover the mountains, to reach the placid waters of the Pacific and to give us a Transcontinental railway when we had a population of less than
8,000,000. We went ahead with that project; in conjunction and co-operation with energetic, far-seeing men the work was carried out and the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed. We saw the vision of a great national system of transportation when we began the expenditure of millions of money for a canal system; up to the 31st of March, 1925, we had .expended $224,000,000 on that work, and it is now part of our transportation system.
We went dtill further; in 1904 the government of the day in its wisdom thought it necessary that we should, in furtherance of that ambitious and courageous policy, construct another Transcontinental line to connect by the shortest possible route the plains, the place of great production on the prairies, with the eastern seaboard and the ports of Quebec and the Maritimes. We spent a great 
deal of money on the project. Some people questioned the wisdom of that policy, but we have now got past the point of its being a debatable question; we have made the expenditure, we have the railway, and we have to face conditions as they are.
We have gone on building up a great transportation system in the country, with one purpose in mind, seeing it from only one point of view, namely, transportation of the products of the west to the eastern seacoast, to give employment to our people, to make traffic for the railways, and to build up business, not only in the west, where they needed transportation, but in the east, as well as to improve conditions at the eastern ports. We continued that policy, and we are forced today, after fifty years, notwithstanding the fact that we have been so courageous as a young country in spending this money, to say that the condition is not satisfactory. Facts have been given to the House in regard to the amount of our shipments of grain through Canadian Atlantic ports, through American ports and through western ports, and the whole consensus of opinion, the whole force of the figures, compel the admission that at the present time the transportation of our products is not proceeding in a satisfactory way and that we are not realizing the vision of the men who started the building of this great transportation system. Instead of our traffic going, as it ought to go, through Canadian channels to Canadian ports for shipment to the markets of the world, it is being diverted or switched off at a tangent to other railways in another country, thereby increasing the traffic on foreign roads and helping to build up the business of a foreign country. There is no occasion to cavil about figures; a million or two bushels do not count one wuy or the other; but it is an established fact that a very large proportion of the products of the farms of Canada, particularly those of the western prairies, is not finding its way through Canadian channels to Canadian ports but is being diverted through American channels to American ports.
Some figures which I gave in the House some time ago on this subject were questioned, and perhaps I should apologize to the House; my figures were absolutely correct except that I used the word "grain" when I should have said wheat. I am sure you will admit, Mr. Speaker, that in the case of a new member on his feet for the first time in the House of Commons the mistake was a pardonable one. I made the mistake, however, and I do not quarrel with the reporter, because I probably used the word "grain" when I should

have said "wheat." But my Statement was entirely correct so far as it applied to Canadian wheat being shipped through Canadian ports and Canadian wheat being shipped through American ports; I was discussing nothing else and intended to discuss nothing else. I was making no reference to our shipments through Pacific Canadian ports. I always try and I always intend to try to be careful in any figures I give, and I was really concerned about it when my figures were questioned in this House. I knew I was on solid ground, because I had taken the figures from the report of the Royal Grain inquiry Commission; the exact figures will be found on pages 217, 203, and 204 of that report. That fact Stands out in all its glaring intensity; we have to confront it, and we in this House should deal with it in some substantial way.

Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was referring to the great advance that had been- made in in this country during the past fifty years in establishing and building up a vast system of transportation. I was trying to point out in-my humble way the vision which the men who preceded us in parliament, the men who had to do with national movements in this country at the time of confederation, had of establishing in this land a great system of transportation which would run east and west and which would carry the ever increasing traffic of the western prairies along Canadian channels to Canadian ports in the east for shipment abroad. I said just before six o'clock that we had been disappointed in this transportation system that had been established at so great a cost, a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars; that it had failed largely to carry out the object for which the money was spent and the transportation provided.
In further evidence of that I want to give the percentages of shipments through United States and Canadian ports respectively for the years 1921, 1922 and 1923; and I am reading from the report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission the memorandum submitted by Mr. Scott at the request of the
commission. He points out, giving the figures in bushels for the year 1921-22 and making a comparison between United States and Canadian seaports, that the exports of Canadian wheat in that year amounted to 74 per cent through United States ports and 26 per cent through Canadian ports. For the next year, the crop year of 1922-23, he gives the figures in bushels and I shall not trouble the House with them; but he again states the percentages: in that year we shipped 65 per cent of our grain products through United States ports and 35 per cent through Canadian ports. Coming down to the year ended 31st August, 1924, he gives the figures in bushels again, and shows that 66 per cent of our grain went through United States Atlantic ports and only 34 per cent through Canadian Atlantic ports. Those figures tell concisely the story of the failure of our great transportation systems to do the thing we had hoped they would do, its failure to accomplish for us the thing that would justify so tremendous an expenditure of public money in their construction.
The resolution presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) deals with one particular part of the great transportation system, the Transcontinental railway. Nowhere else is the failure more absolute and complete than it is in connection with grain traffic on the Transcontinental railway system. The result is far from reaching the vision of that man of high ideals and noble purposes who conceived the idea of having the shortest possible railway route from the prairie provinces to Atlantic seaports, and it has failed entirely to justify the feeling that was held at that time, not only by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government but by this parliament and this country, that we would have at least one system of railway built to a high standard, with the best of grades, the best of curvatures, to carry successfully traffic from the west to the east. But it has failed, and I want to point out that there was no question in regard to the intention or the reason advaned for our making such a tremendous expenditure. Let us in this parliament consider that upon this one line of transportation, the Transcontinental railway, we expended over $165,000,000, and in addition to that we spent over $15,000,000 to build the Quebec bridge; in other words, more than $180,000,000 was spent out of the public treasury in establishing this line of communication. It was to do a great work, and that great work was set out clearly in the agreement made between the government

I am going to read a paragraph dealing directly with the particular matter to which I refer, being part of chapter 71 of the act of the parliament of Canada, assented to on the 24th October, 1903, containing the contract as it was executed between the government of the day and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. This is the section:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada-

Note the words "the express purpose." That ought to be clear enough; it is the express reason why the government granted the aid. This is what the company agreed to:
The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.

We are told that if the statutory rates west of Fort William are made to apply east of Fort William, we shall have a rate war with the railways of the United States. I ask this parliament, in all seriousness: Are we to consider what action the United States railways may take when we are considering such a vital question as the transportation policy of this country? Are we to sacrifice the vision of the men who built this nation, of those who were here at its birth and laid the foundations better than they knew? Shall we sacrifice the vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his party when they constructed the Transcontinental? I say no. Put the railway to work, to do the thing it was built to do.
I said that we should have in this country a sound Canadian transportation policy, a policy that will take our traffic from the west along Canadian channels to the east. That has been the vision of the great men of this country from confederation down to the present. We have heard a great deal during this session about the difficulties of the coal industry in Nova Scotia. Let me point out to the House that if you carry the grain and the cattle of the west by an all-Canadian route to Canadian ports on the Atlantic you will help greatly to remedy the coal situation in the Maritime provinces, and particularly the province of Nova Scotia. They have a market for their coal as long as they can ship it by water, but in the winter season, when shipment is no longer possible by the St. Lawrence, they cannot find a market for it, and that is the time of year when employment in the mines is lessened, when the mines run only two or three days a week, bringing hardship to the coal mining areas of that province. But if we would ship the products of the west to St. John and Halifax, vessels would be leaving our ports practically every day of the week carrying grain, and each vessel would require in her bunkers from one thousand to twelve hundred tons of coal. That would provide a local market for our coal-a market where there would be no question about transportation rates-with resulting great benefit to the coal industry of Nova Scotia.

I said that the carrying out of this sound Canadian policy would bring business to the east. The revival of business and the stimulus that would be given by this traffic would be very great, and it would be felt in many ways. Let me give you an illustration. The arteries *in our body carry the life-sustaining, strength-producing blood to every part of the human system, and so, in a similar way, our railways and our canals are the great arteries through which should flow in undiminished, yea, in *ever increasing quantities, the life-giving commerce of this great country. Going a step further with the simile, if one part of the human body fails to receive the life-sustaining, strength-producing blood, what will happen? That part of the body will become weak and unable to perform its proper function. It is exactly the same with our transportation, and that is just what has happened, Mr. Speaker. We take the increasing commerce of the west and carry it along Canadian channels up to a certain point, but at that point we allow it to be switched off to American railways, to be taken to American ports, to build up the business of American railways and American ports. The result is that the invigorating, life-giving commerce of this country, with its stimulating power on our whole business life, is lost to this country; it is switched off at a tangent and goes on foreign steel to foreign ports. Let us carry it to our own ports, and then the benefit of that life-giving stream will be felt in every part and parcel of eastern Canada, in every city and town of the Maritime provinces.
I do not want to detain the House at too great length. I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to show two or three things. I have tried* to show that the railways are doing very well handling grain at the statutory rate that is in force west of Fort William. I have tried to show that this traffic flowing steadily to the east, to the ports of the province of Quebec and the Maritime ports of Canada, would increase the business of the whole of eastern Canada, and would bring prosperity to parts of eastern Canada that now have great reason to complain. The vision of the men who founded confederation was that the ports of the Maritime provinces should be the great entrepot for the commerce of-what
do you think?-for the commerce of half a continent. That has not materialized. After careful consideration of all the evidence submitted, your committee is of opinion that there exists a most serious condition of affairs, with regard to the diversion of the western grain trade to New York and other United States seaports, for export. There seems to be no doubt that two-thirds, and probably four-fifths of that trade takes that route, and that we are paying many millions annually to United States railways, lake carriers and elevators, that would be earned by our own railways and train men, if it were possible to export this grain at Canadian seaports. Since this evidence was taken, and at the present writing, government statistics show that the diversion still continues, and that of the bountiful crop of 1921 no less than 99 million bushels of wheat went from Fort William to Buffalo.
After all the sacrifices that Canada has made in building three transcontinental railways, it is impossible that we should go on allowing our seaports to be deprived of their legitimate traffic, to obtain which our people have been and are being so heavily taxed. A persistence in this policy must inevitably lead to serious dissatisfaction not only in Quebec and in the Maritime provinces, but also amongst the farmers of the northwest, who will soon realize that these hostile railway tariffs are imposing a burden upon them which they are not called upon to bear.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure every hon.
member will be glad if anything can be done to bring about a greater use of our railroads from coast to coast. I understand the question of railway rates has been submitted again to the Board of Railway Commissioners and I hope that commission will be able to bring in some recommendations or make some arrangements whereby the traffic of this country will flow more freely on our railways from the Pacific to the Atlantic and vice versa. I shall not at this time go into the question of railway rates in any detail because I am satisfied that the commission .will have greater opportunity and better facilities for getting information than I can have.
One thing that strikes me in this debate is that no speaker yet that I have heard-I was not in the chamber all the afternoon- has discussed this question along the lines that it has been discussed outside of the House. Every speaker seems to want to offer some concrete suggestion so that our railroads may be able to carry freight at a reduced rate. That is a little different from that which we have heard during the past two years. We have had some gentlemen, more especially a few lawyers from Winnipeg, going around the country, and "instead of offering concrete or useful suggestions the only thing they seemed to be able to do was to argue that railway rates cannot be reduced because the wages of the railway men were too high and were responsible for the high freight rates. I am glad we have reached the point of realizing that that is not the case and are now trying to find the real solution.
In the discussion of this railroad problem we must not forget that Canadian railroads are handicapped to a large extent as compared with United States railroads. It is, of course, always necessary to compare one organization with another in order to see how we are faring ourselves, and the only system that we can compare ours with is the United States railway system. The British system, the European systems, are equipped to carry light loads short distances, while United States railroads like our own are equipped to carry heavy loads long distances, so that if our railroads compare favourably with those of the United States in operation, efficiency and freight rates, we are at least not doing too badly. But. even at that, Canadian railroads are handicapped, and one of the greatest handicaps is the fact that in Canada we have only about 221 people to each mile of railroad while in the United States they have about 450 people to each mile of railroad.
This is a great factor because we have not density of traffic, and over the whole railroad system it lessens the average earning power. We have again of course severe climatic conditions to contend with. Throughout a great portion of the western country railroad operation has to be carried on with the temperature at from ten to sixty degrees below zero. This not only makes it much more difficult to carry on transportation during the winter season but involves greater cost than in the warmer climates of the United States. In 1924 it cost the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways about four and a half million dollars to clear snow off their tracks. A further handicap is that our railways have about $100,125,000 invested in rolling stock which is in use for only about three months in every year for the movement of the grain crop; during the remainder of the year it is stored on side tracks and is deteriorating more or less. All these are serious handicaps that our Canadian railways have to contend against as compared with the railways of the United States.
But notwithstanding these severe handicaps our freight rates, generally speaking are lower than those prevailing in the United States. This surely denotes efficient management and loyal co-operation of all branches of our railway employees. This is evidenced by the fact that according to statistics each Canadian railway employee moves approximately 12,000 tons of freight per mile more than his fellow worker on the United States roads. It will no doubt be interesting to hon. members to have these comparative figures: to move a ton of freight in Canada five employees are required; a similar number in the United States; twenty-three in Germany; twenty-four in Italy; thirty-one in Switzerland. This is further evidence of the efficient and loyal co-operation of our railway employees with their officers.
I am glad that during the discussion not one hon. member has suggested that the earning power of our railways should be decreased below the amount necessary to maintain a proper rate of wage. I do not think any hon. member would take such a stand, but it has been advocated outside the House. In this connection it must not be forgotten that for the past two years the wages of our railway-men have been about five per cent below those paid in the United States. Therefore it is not to be expected that hon. members either in the House or outside Should advocate a reduction of wages of railwaymen. Our men proved their loyalty in 1921 when they were promised that if they would accept a decrease in their wages the cost of living would come

Transcontinental-Freight Rate
[DOT]down proportionately, and they would thus be recouped. They (took this course, which meant a saving to our railway companies of $45,000,000 annually, but there has as yet been no corresponding decrease in the cost of living.
Few hon. members realize the conditions under which many of our railwaymen have to cany on their very arduous and responsible duties. Usually when someone wishes to disseminate propaganda about Ithe high wages of railwaymen he takes one or two cheques paid to men on some preferred run and probably earned during a rush of coal or wheat, involving working very long hours with very little rest. Suppose these cheques run about $300, they are exhibited to the country as typical of the average rate of wages paid our railwaymen. I suppose very few hon. members realize that over sixty per cent of our railwaymen do not work more than four months in every year; they are employed during the wheat rush and are then laid off, at a time, unfortunately, when other industries are cutting down their staff. Consequently there is no opportunity for the railwayman to get other employment, and he has to rely on his earnings during the rush season of three or four months to maintain himsellf and his family for the whole year. During the last two years about 25,000 fewer employees have been working on our railways, a reduction brought about by greater efficiency of operation and improved motive power, all tending to eliminate the human element. At the present time we have men with twenty-three years' standing as firemen and engineers and trainmen on western lines who cannot get a job even at wiping engines, and there is no prospect of their securing employment until the wheat starts again. Under these conditions it is only natural that our men should begin to think it is about time the railway companies took care of their reserve force. These men are necessary to handle our commerce during the peak periods, and therefore some means should be provided to give them steady employment the whole year round.
I just rose to give these few facts before the debate closed. I am sorry I was not in the House when the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution was speaking. I have a great deal of work to attend to in my office; unfortunately the Premier of Ontario has not seen fit to bring on a by-election to fill the vacancy created by my resignation in the Legislature, and consequently the people of New Ontario are writing to me about provincial affairs.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, from these quotations that it is clearly recognized all the way from Vancouver to Halifax that the Transcontinental railway is not being used for the purpose for which it was constructed. When we think of Canadian grain, Canada's largest basic product, flowing through American territory and building up American seaports to the detriment of our own Canadian seaports, it seems to me it is about time the Canadian people came to the full realization of the real intention in the construction of this great undertaking. The commercialized idea of turning the railroads into a profit-making undertaking, irrespective of the parliamentary commitments, seems to be the main idea of those who have charge of the National railways in this country to-day. While we are not advocating that the railways should carry our products free, we are advocating that, by carrying our products east and west, they should create an east and west policy by reduction in rates which will in the end build up a volume of trade that will more than offset any slight loss that may be incurred at the outset. The natural trend of trade in the Dominion of Canada is north and south. The north and south trade will develop itself, because that is the natural channel in which trade will flow in this country unless we direct it otherwise, but we must develop the east and west traffic, and the only way in which we can develop it is by allowing our products to seek outlets on the seaboards of this country, both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific and not in a foreign country. But if we continue the policy that has been followed for the past number of years, of allowing the great quantity of our largest basic product, the grain of this country, to flow through American ports, to the detriment of our own, then it seems to me that all the parliamentary commitments and all the statements of the legislators in 1903 and 1904 bearing on the building of the Transcontinental will have been violated, and we shall be violating the commercial interests of this country in a general sense unless this policy being advocated by the mover of the resolution is taken hold of and very ardently pushed forward to a successful application by the parliament of this Dominion.
I said the other day, when speaking to the resolution introduced by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), that it would appear from the attitude of the railway authorities that there is only one body in the Dominion of Canada that is capable of dealing with the railway problem, so far as the general policy

of keeping Canadian trade on Canadian railways is concerned, and that body is the parliament of Canada. It is true that the railways of this country have just had a splendid year, and we are all very happy in the knowledge of that fact; it is certainly a great incentive to the railways as a publicly-owned institution, and the showing that has been made is to be heartily commended. But, Mr. Speaker, there is still a deficit. As I understand the figures, the fixed charges of our National Railways amount to about $70,000,000, but I understand that we only have to pay out on account of fixed charges about $40,000,000, and that the real deficit in dollars and cents, outside of the bookkeeping aspect of the matter, is between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000. Now if the deficits have been reduced to that figure, which is not very alarming in view of some of the former deficits on this road, it seems to me that the parliament of Canada will be very well advised to instruct those in authority in connection with the railways that further reductions should be made in the rates to promote this east and west traffic, so important to every portion of Canada and every interest in Canada. While some sacrifice may be necessary on the part of the whole Dominion to ensure this trade flowing the way it should flow, and at the rate at which it was intended to flow, in accordance with the commitments of parliament, and with the statements of those who brought the matter forward in 1903 and 1904, I am convinced that that sacrifice will be cheerfully made by all Canadians.
In closing I beg to repeat that I am in hearty accord with the resolution as proposed by the hon. member for Mackenzie in its general application.

I rise for a moment or two to speak to this resolution. I am not going to discuss the resolution as a whole or at length. I do desire, however, to bring to the attention of the House one or two features, and to move an amendment by way of addition which will not in any sense, I think, interfere with the resolution as it now stands but will add a clause to it.
I may remind the House that a year ago, or almost so, when a similar question was before it in the form of a bill fixing rates by statute, and on other occasions prior to that I declared that so far as I was concerned I was opposed to parliament taking upon itself the responsibility of fixing rates. I think it is a bad principle. I have always thought so and I am still of that opinion. Furthermore, on

that occasion I pointed out to the government that if, in the bill which was brought before the House last year, they insisted on fixing the rates it would undoubtedly be followed at future times with demands for fixing rates in other sections or upon other lines, and the resolution now before us is simply a fulfilment of that prophecy, if I may so term it. I still adhere to the principle that parliament should not fix rates but should determine the main principles upon which rates should be fixed, and then leave the actual determination of those rates to a competent body, a body such as the railway board. I still believe that is the right course to pursue. For many years we in British Columbia have been suffering from very unfair and discriminatory rates. However, while I have realized that, I have consistently urged that our appeal ought to be to the railway board, the body properly constituted for the study and determination of this important question. But I confess that many of my fellow-citizens have been disappointed in the apparent slowness with which these matters have been dealt with, and they feel that something should be done to hasten the lowering of rates on various commodities moved to and from the Pacific coast. I will only take sufficient of the time of the House to put myself on record as supporting the resolution introduced by the hon. membdr for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and so ably supported by other hon. members. For many years the railway rate on grain shipped westward from the prairie provinces was prohibitive. Grain shipped westward had only to travel 700 miles to the Pacific ocean, while eastward it had to go two-thirds of the way accross the continent. This discrimination in rates complained of has been largely removed. The last speaker has said that he wanted the discrimination removed also as far as westward shipments were concerned, but as stated I think that has largely been done. The rates westward from the prairie provinces are now almost on the same mileage basis as the rates eastward to Fort William. From Alberta it costs 20 cents per hundred pounds to ship grain to Vancouver and 26 cents per hundred pounds to ship to Fort William, a distance of 1,350 miles. But upon reaching Fort William there is a change, and discrimination once more obtains. Although the rate from the prairies to Fort William is 26 cents per hundred, a distance of 1,350 miles, a rate of 34J-cents is charged from Fort William to Quebec, a distance of 1,000 miles. At any time the railway board or the government or someone in authority explains to us why that is so, I suppose these arguments will cease, but until it is shown why a railway that was built for the express purpose of carrying grain by the shortest route with the best grades to the Atlantic shore is

Transcontinental-Freight Rate
not used for that purpose, I presume the arguments will continue in this House. If the grain will not go over that route when rates are fixed on the same mileage basis as in other parts of the country; if it goes southward through other ports, then we will have nothing to say; but so adjust the rates as to give the road a chance. There is no use in building, a road for this trade and then making the rates prohibitive. Under present conditions the people of the Maritime provinces cannot expect the grain to go through their ports. I am sure all hon. members who have spoken desire that the rate should be fixed on the same mileage basis as in other parts of the Dominion. My argument is that wherever the grain is placed upon the train, at any station in the Dominion, the mileage rates should be the same. If that is done we shall have no complaint, because the grain will flow to the natural port.
We in western Canada know that all our grain will not go to the Pacific ocean. We do not expect it all to go there. At times it will go westward; at other times it will go eastward, and when it goes eastward we would like equal rates on the mileage basis, so that we would all get (the benefit of it. I am sure this proposition will appeal to all parts of the Dominion; Nova Scotia, Quebec and all the other provinces will want it. I do not know what part of the country would oppose it. The railway board have the matter before them, but if the House will give attention to these questions it might be of some assistance. I do not think we are exceeding our privileges in debating this matter in the House.
I am fully convinced, as was stated by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) that the undertaking and purpose [DOT]for which the road' was built should be carried out, that the shortest route with the best grade should be adopted and the road given a fair chance to compete with other lines, thus giving us the benefit of real competition. If all these conditions were fulfilled and the road could not compete, then we would have nothing to say, because the people will have got what they asked for namely, the compensation of real competition. I wish to endorse the resolution so ably presented by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and so well supported by all hon. members who have spoken.

Mr. Speaker, the cattle trade is interested in this resolution. The resolution reads:
Whereas the fulfilment of this purpose has been prevented by the imposition of exorbitant and unjustifiable freight rates; and

Whereas the port of Quebec has exceptional advantages as a shipping point for export cattle, which advantages are lost to the grower owing to the impossibility of making up mixed cargoes in the absence of a steady supply of grain for export.
I am pleased that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) was kind enough to include the cattle with the grain, because they should be associated. Having been in that trade for a number of years and having travelled over the Transcontinental, I may tell the House that it is an excellent road, that there are splendid facilities at Quebec for loading cattle, that there should be more cattle coming out of the western country over that road for export, and that cattle should be carried over the line as well as grain. I am glad the lion. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is in his seat, because he has heard me before on this subject and I may tell him that it is impossible to bring cattle over that road to the seaboard and then pay a $20 rate on live stock to Great Britain. We have twenty-four ships of the merchant marine of 8,000 tons capacity, and, with a very little fitting these would be admirably suited for carrying live stock. But when the cattle get to the seaboard and have to face a $20 rate it is an absolute impossibility for the western men to raise cattle on that basis. The government must do something in regard to transportation by ocean before they deal with the Transcontinental rates.
In regard to the Transcontinental, I do not believe any of us are giving credit to that company and to the other railway companies for the service they are giving. We are getting magnificent service, far better than we ever got in the old days. In western Canada on one occasion I had five hundred cattle ready to ship, at Yorkton. The boat was held at Montreal or Quebec and I had to pay $100 a day demurrage. To-day there is no trouble to get cars; they are making wonderful running time over both these roads, they are giving wonderful service. But you cannot pay the freight rates by rail and ocean . The trade is dwindling in western Canada as the hon. Minister of Agriculture knows. Hon. members of this House will bear me out in that statement, because they know very well that the live stock industry has no chance to do business with the exorbitant charges that are made. The rate is now 85 cents a hundred, as compared with 60i cents per hundred thirty-five years ago. After the road was completed in 1885 I had the honour of taking the first shipment over that road, it cost 60i cents a hundred based on a Winnipeg rate. They asked at that time for fourteen cars for train lot. Now you have 72 cars leaving Winnipeg

and the rate is So cents per hundred, and there are many different things in the way of charges added before the cattle reach shipboard, to say nothing about the $20 rate on the ocean. Before they reach shipboard dozens of things are charged against them now which were not charged in the old days. They charged 6(B cents a hundred with five of a crew drawing fourteen cars. To-day five men take 72 cars out of Winnipeg and as stated the rate is 85 cents-they say it is labour. Mr. Speaker, it is not labour, the increased tonnage helps to pay that. Labour was kind enough to concede 10 per cent of its wages towards giving us a reduction in the freight on live stock, and on other products going over the road. We never got that 10 per cent. It is no use trying to foster the cattle industry, which is mentioned in this resolution-and with that I am absolutely in accord-so long as present conditions exist. I appeal to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke)-I cannot see whether he is in his seat or not, but he could tell them in one minute whether or not there will be a $15 rate. He knows he is master of the situation, and if he is imbued with too much grain and cannot look after the cattle industry I hold him responsible. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite or to hon. gentle-ment on this side, whichever may have control. that we must have such a rate that this business will not' be driven out of existence. The hon. gentleman, as I have stated is master of the situation and can and should demand such a rate in fairness and justice to the people of western Canada.
The port of Quebec is an admirable port to ship out of and I have used it many times as a shipping port; the Transcontinental is a good railway and gives good service; it is all we ask for; but the oppressive rates we cannot stand with regard to moving live stock to the markets of the world. I have been charged with being a monomaniac and also talking too much in Marquette on this transportation question, but it is the real question that is holding back the live stock business in Canada. Write down the capitalization, $2,000,000,000, of the Canadian National to equal that of the Canadian Pacific railway; spread the debt over the whole country; let us take our loss and let the man in charge operate it so that it can earn money. Then say to him: Effect economies and manage the railway in the same way as the Canadian Pacific is managed. In that manner we can have some redress.
I do not want to take up the time of the House. I have had my orders to speak briefly. My constituents have told me: Never
read your speech; get up and say what you have to say in the House. On behalf of the live stock industry I say that something must be done in connection with rail and ocean transportation, also grain and other commodities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Many times in this House have the claims of British Columbia been urged in connection wth equalization of freight rates. From time immemorial we have been discriminated against by reason of our mountains; the mountain scale has operated against British Columbia. I think it was in 1920 that the mountain scale was reduced so that it stood one and one-quarter to one, and that is where it stands to-day, with the exception of rates on grain and flour moving from Alberta and Saskatchewan to the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert.
In 1922 members from British Columbia in this party pleaded with the government to leave the whole question to the Board of Railway Commissioners and not to introduce statutory freight rates. The government refused and they introduced statutory freight rates on grain and flour moving from prairie points eastward to Fort William. It was at that point that the government got itself into a. hopeless mess in regard to freight rates. In 1923 this question of statutory freight rates was again debated in the House and a plea was then made on behalf of British Columbia that the same treatment should be given to that province as had been given the year before to the prairie provinces. British Columbia was discriminated against in that year not only by the mountain scale but by rates on grain and flour, which meant that freight rates from prairie points to Vancouver were almost twice as great as freight rates for equal distances going eastward.
Later on, I think it was in 1924, the Crows-nest pass agreement came into complete effect, and in that year British Columbia was further discriminated against by reason of the fact that Ontario fruit farmers could ship their fruit from the Niagara district as far west as Calgary at as low a freight rate as the Okanagan fruit grower could ship his fruit from Vernon, British Columbia, to Calgary, about one-third or one-fourth the distance. In 1925, by a stroke of fortune, the Board of Railway Commissioners held the Crowsnest pass agreement to be practically a nullity and ultra vires of parliament, and parliament had its opportunity then to get
2598	COMMONS
Transcontinental-Freight Rate
rid of statutory freight rates once and for all. But no; this government once more introduced statutory freight rates on grain and flour eastward. "When they introduced the bill the same rates were given on grain and flour from the prairie provinces westward to Vancouver, but when pressure was brought to bear on this government by the big interests, by the railway corporations, the government quickly removed its measure of justice to British Columbia and inserted in the measure a provision which denied those rights to that province.
Since that time the Board of Railway Commissioners has handed down a judicial decision which has given some measure of relief to British Columbia on grain and flour, but the discrimination is not completely ironed out, although I have no doubt the government would attempt to claim credit for the decision of a judicial body. It has been claimed that this government has attempted to dictate to that judicial body, and an explanation might well be forthcoming in parliament of the dictation of the government to that judicial body, something that is unpardonable on the part of any government in connection with judicial matters.
It may be thought by some members from the Maritime provinces and other parts of Canada who are not familiar with the situation in British Columbia, that because of these mountains there should be higher rates. Many years ago Britidi Columbia guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway from Edmonton to Vancouver on the express condition and agreement that, in consideration of that guarantee, British Columbia would have control of freight rates over that railway. Unfortunately the war came on and by an act- of this parliament the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners was given control of rates on the Canadian Northern railway and although we had guaranteed the bonds and our guarantee stands on those bonds, the right of control over freight rates on the Canadian Northern railway was taken away from us. Despite the fact that the Canadian Northern railway from Edmonton to Vancouver has a grade equal to grades in any part of the prairies and superior to grades in any part of eastern Canada, the term "mountain scale" is still applied to that railway in British Columbia and that province has been consistently discriminated against, notwithstanding the fact that that railway was built on the initiative and the guarantee of British Columbia and would not have been built had it not been for that guarantee.

It might also be pointed out that British Columbia was the only province in Canada to contribute a very large acreage of land towards the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. It was one of the terms of union between British Columbia and the Dominion that the province should convey the railway belt, comprising twenty miles of land on each side of the Canadian Pacific railway, and a large area known as the Peace river belt, to the Dominion government in trust to be used in aid of the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. When that railway was completed all of these lands had not been used. By their loud conversation I take it that members of the government are not interested and prefer to ignore the claims of British Columbia. Of course I suppose they think, "Well, it is only British Columbia." Such an attitude is natural on the part' of a government of which Saskatchewan has three members and Ontario only one. The claims of British Columbia do not matter to the government. They have our lands and they will give statutory freight rates, no doubt whenever it suits their purpose, but will pay as little attention as they possibly can to those provinces that are not represented in the cabinet. But for the benefit of those private members who are interested in the case of British Columbia, I would point out that a previous government, the government of which my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) was the head, recognized the justice of our claims and in Cctober, 1920, passed an order in council containing the following:
The committee of the privy council therefore further recommend that as conditions have probably changed materially in recent years, tending more and more to make equalization practicable, an inquiry by the board be directed to be held at the earliest date with a view to the establishment of rates meeting to the utmost extent possible the above requirement a3 to equalization.
That recommendation, it is true, was directed to the Board of Railway Commissioners, but so far as members from British Columbia are concerned I am quite sure we have always been content to have the claims of our province considered by the judicial body which was constituted for that purpose. However, we do submit that we are entitled to receive the same treatment as the other provinces, and if they are given special statutory rates I claim that British Columbia is likewise entitled to such rates.
I submit that British Columbia more than any other province can offer the strongest possible case to parliament for consideration, for it has contributed to a very large extent

Mr. Speaker, as a representative of the district of Quebec and as a citizen of the city of Quebec, I am in full sympathy with the principle of this resolution and I wish to extend to its mover my very hearty thanks for having brought the matter before the House. I need not stress the very vital importance of this question in so far as the city of Quebec and our section of the country are concerned.
