This resolution mentions the construction of the Transcontinental railway and the main purpose of that undertaking. I remember listening to our late lamented leader Sir Wilfrid Laurier when, during the election of 1904, addressing his constituents in the city of Quebec, he expressed the hopes which he thought would be realized by the building of this line from the Pacific to the Atlantic ocean. Circumstances which are well known to members of this House have so far prevented the full realization of those very high hopes, and I have no doubt that every hon. member, no matter to what party he may belong, will help to his utmost to realize the hopes which were entertained at the time the construction of the National Transcontinental was endorsed by the people of Canada. Nothing would please the people of Quebec so much as to see this great scheme of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the scheme that he thought would be the main achievement of his political career, carried to completion.
As far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we will always be ready to co-operate with our western friends, and with our friends from any other section of Canada, to develop the shipping trade in the harbour of Quebec, for we think that by doing so we are not only performing a task which will help
us locally, but which in the main will be of national importance, because the harbour of Quebec on account of its facilities and its situation is really a great national port in the fullest acceptance of the word.

Mr. E. P. Mallory of the Canadian National Railways also stated that the present cost of grain movement over the line was 6-28 mills per ton mile, allowing for the return of empty cars to Fort William. So far as the evidence is available, then, it would seem that the Canadian National Railways are losing about $6,000,000 each year in the carrying of grain to Fort William at less than the actual cost of that traffic.
This is a very important matter upon which parliament should have full information, and I would suggest to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) that this resolution might be referred to the standing committee on Railways and Canals in order that the officials of the National railway system might be examined, and that parliament, through the committee, might be fully informed as to these facts. If parliament in its wisdom has fixed by statute a rate to Fort William which entails a loss to the government of this country, urfler present conditions, of $6,000,000 a year, we should be informed of that fact before we are in a position to discuss whether or not a similar reduction should be made on freight rates to Quebec or to the Pacific coast. I would suggest that this is a matter to which the railway committee might devote a certain portion of its time, because from the statements made in this House it is clear that there is a division of opinion regarding certain allegations, which may be sustained or refuted by the evidence.
I would also like to refer to the fact that the freight carried on the railways of Canada is not wheat alone. Our western friends seem to think that the wheat traffic is the greater traffic of the railways of Canada, but I notice from the return for 1925 made by the railways that in a total freight of 96,239,379 tons

Wood, the foreign freight traffic manager of that line, gave evidence before the select committee of the United States Shipping Board at Washington, in which he said:
The traffic which comes through the port of Portland is. I should say, without going into exact figures, possibly 80 or 90 per cent of Canadian origin. The port of Portland has been practically built up by the Grand Trunk Railway, and largely from Canadian traffic. There are other lines coming to Portland, of course, besides the White Star Dominion, but we [DOT] fMr. Cahan.]

The suggestion was made-and I think it is clear-that the Canadian National Railways are under obligation to find tonnage for the White Star-Dominion line at Portland, because in his evidence as reported Mr. Wood says:
If that service were not there, I do not know where it would be: most likely it would come to St. John, Ne,v Brunswick.
Then he added that the contract may be terminated on six months' notice, such notice to be given before March 1 of the calendar year. So that we find ourselves in this situation, that the Canadian National railway is carrying millions of bushels of grain to Portland to supply these White Star-Dominion liners with freight across the Atlantic according to contract in force between the steamship line and the railway company.
Now I would like to call attention to another fact. We have at Fort William and Port Arthur an elevator capacity of something like 63,500,000 bushels. WTe have at the bay ports, so-called, at Tiffin, Port McNicoll, Midland, Depot Harbour and Goderich, all in Ontario, an elevator capacity of some 16,550,000 bushels. Then we have the elevators at Port Colborne and Buffalo on Lake Erie, and elevators at Montreal and Quebec city on the St. Lawrence. I can well understand that the 'all-water route from the west from Port Arthur to Montreal or Quebec would be a cheaper route to operate during the summer months than the rail route to either of those ports, but when navigation is closed on the lakes and on the St. Lawrence, then the fact is, I am informed, that the same rate is given by rail from Fort William and the same rate is given by rail from the so-called bay ports in Ontario, to each of the Atlantic ports, including Halifax, St. John West or St. John City, Portland, New York, Norfolk, Virginia, or Baltimore, and that when the shipment of grain ceases by the water route, then, under the rates which now exist over the Canadian National lines, you have exactly the same rate to Halifax or St. John as you have to any of these other Atlantic ports; but as a matter of fact the grain finds its way to

these Atlantic ports in the United States for shipment all during the winter months. Now the reason it went to American ports, it is suggested, is because shippers over the National railways preferred American ports to Canadian ports, although the freight rate over the railways was exactly the same. I would think it very interesting indeed for a committee of this House to have Sir Henry Thornton and these gentlemen before it, and to ascertain just what are the influences which direct grain from Fort William or from the bay ports over American lines and through American ports, when the same rate is open to them during the whole winter months to the Canadian ports of Halifax and St. John. That is a matter in which the Maritime provinces are very much interested indeed.
I am persuaded that if the Canadian National Railway management really desired to encourage trade east and west; if they really desired, as Sir Henry Thornton said, to build up trade through Canadian ports, that that company, without using any undue influences at all, could direct the greater part of that trade to the Canadian ports of Halifax and St. John during the winter months. I have made all sorts of inquiries, and I am not yet able to convince myself that the shipment of the bulk of that tonnage by American ports is not due to the fact that the Canadian National Railway and its officials are using all the influences which they can control to direct that trade to Portland and other American ports.

The exporter arranges for his ocean tonnage, his ocean space; he buys it as a commodity the same as anything else is bought. He knows when it will be available and at what port. He buys it and the business of the railroad is to take the grain where it is ordered by the

shipper to take it. This criticism, however, centres on the Canadian National; and let me say that I am both a Canadian Pacific and a Canadian National man.

subtopic: MOTION TO REMOVE FREIGHf RATE DISCRIMINATIONS AGAINST THE PORT OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Of course in Chicago the Canadian National as well as the Canadian Pacific are endeavouring to-secure United States grain business for Canadian railroads, and both of them get a great deal of it. I will give the figures to my hon. friend when I get along a little further. It is rather hard on a new and green member of the House to be interrupted, but I welcome interruptions if I can get back to the thread of my subject a little later on. Naturally, in Chicago our railways are endeavouring to secure United States business over Canadian lines, but the shipper of that grain can choose his ocean port and he arranges his own ocean space. The Canadian National probably has in Chi-, cago connections with several brokers who are selling space in ocean vessels calling at a number of Canadian and United States Atlantic ports; but in regard to the general practice in the grain business I can assure my hon. friend that the shipper buys his ocean space and lake space. That is a commodity that is dealt in at Winnipeg, Montreal and, I presume, other ports as well. But as a matter of fact in closing up an export transaction in grain in Winnipeg the shipper tries to tie together three things: the price of the grain in the bin at Fort William, what it will cost him to get it to the ocean ports, and the space on the ship. Those factors are settled so far as price and date are concerned before he can really close the export transaction for his grain.

Now, I should not like the House to get the impression that the railways cannot exert any influence whatever in connection with shipments. I think the moral influence of all our Canadian railways with their shippers should be exerted at all times in the direction of securing shipment for Canadian products-or American products, for that matter-over Canadian railways and through Canadian ports. That is good business for Canada. And with regard to the general question, may I say to my hem. friend from St. Lawrence-St George that if as Minister of Railways I find any tendency on the part of that railway which is most closely connected with the government and with the parliament of Canada to influence shipments through American ports which from the point of view of the shipper might come just as readily through Canadian ports, all the influence which I have will be exerted against that practice. If my hon. friend can offer to me anything beyond the bald statements of bulk figures of Canadian grain which went via American ports-and which by the way include Canadian Pacific as well as Canadian National shipments-as evidence that Sir Henry Thornton-well, I will not go into what my hon. friend said, for there is some difference of opinion as to what he really did say.
With the general principle of the resolution, as I said at the outset, I have no doubt the House is pretty generally agreed. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), in moving his amendment put his finger on the difficulty-I am afraid his amendment increased the difficulty rather than reduced it- when he pointed out that there is a body specially provided by parliament to do this work now investigating this very matter, having at its disposal the services of experts to determine the value of the evidence submitted. This body is charged under the order in council which I read to take such effective action under the Railway Act as it may deem necessary to ensure as far as possible the routing of Canadian grain and other products through Canadian ports.
Much has been said regarding the use of the National Transcontinental for grain shipment. All-rail haulage of grain, judging from past experience, will not likely be a very important portion of the total movement of Canadian grain eastward. There again arises an interesting question on how the business itself is conducted. The desire of the grain shipper is always to get his grain east of the lakes as soon as possible before they freeze up. During the heavy shipping season grain naturally flows down the lakes to Montreal

Tramcontinental-Freight Rate
and other ports. That is the cheapest way. Some of it goes via Georgian bay ports on what is known as the lake-and-rail route at a special rate from bay ports to Montreal during that season of the year. If I remember rightly, the rate when I was in the business was five cents from bay ports to Montreal during the season of navigation on the lakes. Just before the lakes freeze over, the grain exporter makes every effort to get all the grain he possibly can east of the lakes. Why is that? To take care of his winter commitments in Europe and thereby save the extra cost of the allrail haulage around the lakes or otherwise, whichever route is taken. The desire of the trade every year, a very natural desire, is to get sufficient stock stored in the terminal elevators and transfer houses, a list of which was read by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George, in order that being east of the lakes, nearer the sea, they are able to take their grain easily to the Canadian and American Atlantic ports rather than pay the extra cost of the all-rail haul, which everyone sees must be higher than the lake rates.
We have had an investigation recently by the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission touching this matter very closely. The report has been referred to on several occasions during the debate. In this connection I want to place on Hansard some figures which relate to another phase of the subject. Much has been made, and properly so, of the volume of Canadian grain which passes through American ports, but it is not generally known that there is a very large amount of American grain going through Canadian ports. I have here some figures from my department regarding the matter. I find that in the crop year of 1921-22, 89,573.000 bushels of American grain passed through Canadian ports.

speechtext:
I will give my hon.
friend the reasons on authority possibly better than my own. The Royal Grain Inquiry Commission looked into this matter, and I think its report is now regarded in the grain trade and in railway circles as a text book upon the subject of grain handling in Canada. The information contained in that report is generally regarded by growers and shippers as pretty authentic; there may be differences of opinion with regard to minor matters, but in general the report is the most complete compendium on the subject now extant. This is what the report says touching this matter, at page 145:
Canadian and American ports:
While shipments of grain from Montreal make it tiie leading grain port of the north Atlantic, it is well known that a large proportion of the grain shipped from there comes from the United States. On the other hand a large part of the Canadian export grain goes through the port of New York or other north Atlantic United States ports. There is a simple explanation to this apparently paradoxical situation. At all times grain will flow along the cheapest route to the Old World entrepots. It is very sensitive to variations in freight rates. The rates that must be considered are not merely the Atlantic freight and insurance rates but the total of rates from the western terminals on the Great Lakes to the ports of entry on the other side of the Atlantic.
That is exactly the point I was making a few moments ago.
When this is considered a net difference of a sixpence a ton in favour of one route over the other will attract the traffic.
Latter on in the same report at page 146, dealing with the same matter, I find the following:
We are now in a position to point to certain conditions which govern the flow of grain during the course of the year to these ports. The American harvest matures several weeks earlier than the Canadian. As a result, the advantages of the St. Lawrence route at-

Transcontinerital-Freight Rate
tract heavy shipments from American lake terminals to Montreal. By the time the flow of Canadian grain begins to assume volume a large part of the American export of grain has been accomplished. On the other hand, on account of the lateness of the Canadian crop, the end of the grain shipping season is approaching on the St. Lawrence, before it does at the head of the lakes. This fact is of great significance as explaining partly why so much Canadian grain goes via New York and other American North Atlantic ports. When the flow of Canadian grain is still vigorous, navigation on the St. Lawrence ceases. Commonly it closes about two weeks earlier than navigation on the Great Lakes.
That is a very important factor in connection with this whole matter. The movement eastward over the Great Lakes is facilitated, but the grain is prevented from going out by the port of Montreal.

speechtext:
I am afraid any answer to that question might possibly produce an argument among my hon. friends from the province of Quebec. There may be some difference between the relative availability of the two ports, but in general, as applying to St. Lawrence navigation, this statement is time. Taking the general average of movement down the Great Lakes and the movement out of St. Lawrence ports, what is stated here is true. I continue quoting:
Hence the flow of grain for this latter period is deflected towards Buffalo or the Georgian bay or lower lake ports from whence it will move to tide water by rail. The end of the season finds these bay, lower lake and Buffalo elevators filled with grain which will move out gradually during the winter. The grain carrying fleet on the Great Lakes takes a final cargo for winter storage and a large part of this fleet ties up at Buffalo for the winter. When spring comes, their grain is discharged and moves out chiefly via New York.
In the spring movement one additional factor is of importance. During the winter the bay port and Buffalo elevators have become emptied of their stock in store. The first movement of grain down the lakes in the spring is to these ports as the most expeditious route to tide water. It will thus be seen that the explanation for a large movement of American grain through the port of Montreal and a large movement of Canadian grain through New York and other Un.ted States Atlantic ports rests chiefly on seasonal changes affecting the St. Lawrence route.
It might reasonably be inquired why there is not a considerable movement of grain from the bay ports to St. John and Halifax.
This touches the very point especially emphasized by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.
At present there is some movement in that direction, and at St. John this movement appears to be growing. The obstacles to a larger movement appear to be partly

high freight rates and partly the absence of available cargo space offering at low rates at these seaports. As we have pointed out above, grain is an excellent basic cargo. As traffic grows at Halifax and St. John a laige quantity of cargo space will offer regularly for the transport of grain. When this occurs more grain should move during the winter months through these ports. Lately Halifax has been put on the same insurance basis as New York.
That is an important advance.
This removes one factor which has militated against her in the past.
The situation at Quebec is virtually that of Montreal, with the additional advantage of a longer season.
That confirms what my hon. friend just asked.	-
There does not seem to be any reason why the port of Quebec should not share with Montreal a part of the advantages of the St. Lawrence route. Montreal has developed wide business connections in the grain trade so that the traffic is accustomed to move through this port. It is open to Quebec to do the same thing; no physical obstacles lie in the way of the inauguration of an extensive grain export trade. Indeed, as the capacity of the port of Montreal begins to be taxed at the peak of the movement, a part of the traffic might with advantage move to Quebec. Quebec also enjoys a more favourable insurance rate and is 180 miles nearer to Liverpool than is Montreal.
Then the commission goes into this very matter of freight rates, which of course touches every matter under investigation in connection with that part of Canada, or indeed in connection with the economics of any part of Canada. The freight rate situation has an important bearing upon our national life, and I presume there never has been a commission appointed to look into anything connected with the economics of Canadian business or national life which has not reported in some sense or dwelt, shortly or at some length, with the matter of freight rates. It as of very great importance, touching every subject as it does. Regarding freight rates, the commission has this to say:
Upon several occasions we were asked to recommend that rates be granted on export grain over the Canadian National Railways to Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and St. John, sufficiently low to deflect to them the traffic which now goes by rail to the Atlantic ports of the United States.
These suggestions were made to the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission.
The object sought to be attained is undoubtedly a most worthy one; the preservation of Canadian trade for Canadian ports and the expenditure in Canada of a large amount of money which is now earned annually by United States railways. The subject forms an important part of a still larger question which has engaged the attention of parliament in the past, and is still in the forefront of our national problems which await solution. In 1922, the Senate of Canada investigated the question of the export of Canadian grain and appointed a committee to examine expert witnesses on the subject. Evidence was given by railway officials, shippers, members of the grain trade and other business men.

In its report the committee emphasized the desirability of steps being taken in the national interest to divert this export grain traffic to Canadian ports, and recommended specifically (1) the lowering of rates on the Canadian National Railways, (2) the providing of greater elevator accommodation at Canadian ports, and (3) the making of an arrangement by the government whereby marine insurance rates from Canadian ports might be lowered to meet the rates prevailing from United States ports.
I would here c-all the attention of the House to the fact that real advances have been made in connection with the recommendations of that Senate committee. Marine insurance rates are now on the same basis from Canadian Atlantic ports as from American Atlantic ports; that has been accomplished. With regard to greater elevator accommodation an elevator has been provided at the port of Halifax. That is surely an advance. Then the commission goes on to deal with the evidence placed before it regarding this matter, and admits that it is not competent-I do not know that that is exactly the word used -to determine this question, but suggests that it is a proper matter 'to be investigated by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
I have one or two more points, Mr. Speaker, but I do not intend to keep the House at great length in this matter. The mover of the resolution appeared, quite fairly, to discuss the relationship of this matter to the regular rates prevailing down the lakes, and from Georgian bay ports, to Montreal. He pointed out that in at least two years the 11 cent rate which he was advocating would have proved a regulator of Canadian lake rates on grain. I am sure he would be the first to admit that the condition in question is not a normal one; that it is rather exceptional; that Under normal circumstances we could not ex-Ipect any of this grain to move by rail on an 11 cent rate while the Great Lakes were open. Lower rates would normally prevail by boat down the lakes, or by a lake and rail rate via Georgian bay ports.
